target_learning_goals: character development
examples: The author applies this approach by using the Foundations for Young Adult Success framework to propose ten developmental experiences as mechanisms
key_sources: Key Questions: How might learning environments "build character" in children and youth?. (2017). Journal of Character Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: The Success Project
citation: Cowhy, J.R. & de la Torre, M. (2017). The Success Project: The Implementation and Early Outcomes of a Middle Grade Program. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://uei.uchicago.edu/
title: Protecting curriculum time through principal buy-in and flexible delivery models
description: A lesson-level implementation pattern in which schools secure a stable slot for a non-tested curriculum by obtaining administrator buy-in early and adapting delivery to existing structures. The report found "identifying and protecting time  to teach the 6to16 curriculum within their school schedules was a critical step in implementation." Coordinators succeeded by negotiating schedule changes at the start of the year and by embedding lessons in social studies, MTSS, SEL, homeroom, or prep periods, delivered to whole classes or small groups.
requirements: Principal or administrator buy-in secured at the start-of-year schedule planning
Flexibility to deliver the curriculum to a whole class or a small group
constraints: District accountability pressure privileging tested subjects squeezed out non-tested curriculum time
Where principals did not buy in, 6to16 time was lost, even during testing periods in schools with full buy-in
target_learners: Middle grades students in high-accountability urban elementary schools
target_learning_goals: College readiness knowledge and skills delivered through a non-tested curriculum
examples: One coordinator whose administration fully bought into the program never lost 6to16 time, including during testing windows, after integrating it into the year's systems during start-of-year planning.
key_sources: Cowhy, J.R. & de la Torre, M. (2017). The Success Project: The Implementation and Early Outcomes of a Middle Grade Program. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/success-project-implementation-and-early-outcomes-middle-grade-program

article_title: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement
citation: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement. (2017). Chapter 7 of Teaching in Context: The Social Side of Education Reform, Harvard Education Press. https://www.harvardeducationpress.com
title: Improve schools by creating conditions and structures that let teachers share knowledge and work together effectively
description: The chapter's parent book proposes an alternative to individual-focused teacher quality enhancement: "creating conditions and school structures that facilitate the transmission and sharing of knowledge among teachers, allowing teachers to work together effectively." It rests on evidence that teachers become more effective when organizations support them in comprehensive and coordinated ways, capitalizing on what is known about how educators learn and improve.
requirements: School organizations must support teachers in comprehensive and coordinated ways
target_learners: teachers
school leaders
target_learning_goals: teacher improvement through knowledge transmission and collaborative work
examples: The book's studies feature leading scholars showing teachers become more effective in organizations that support them comprehensively and in coordinated ways.
key_sources: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement. (2017). Chapter 7 of Teaching in Context: The Social Side of Education Reform, Harvard Education Press. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/how-organization-schools-and-local-communities-shape-educational-improvement

article_title: Teacher Evaluation in Practice
citation: Sporte, S.E., & Jiang, J.Y. (2016). Teacher Evaluation in Practice: Year 3 Teacher and Administrator Perceptions of REACH. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/page/teacher-evaluation
title: Policymakers should take participant perceptions of an evaluation reform into account when building on strengths and correcting weaknesses
description: Because an educational reform's success "depends on how individuals involved in that effort interpret and act on that reform," the brief argues participant perceptions are key information about buy-in and implementation. Perceptions identify areas of strength and weakness from the experiences of those living with the system, so policymakers and practitioners should build on positive perceptions while addressing aspects participants see as needing improvement.
requirements: Systematic collection of teacher and administrator perceptions, such as annual surveys of those affected by the reform.
constraints: Survey responses are anonymous, so perceptions cannot be linked to individual evaluation ratings.
target_learners: Teachers and school administrators in districts implementing new evaluation systems
target_learning_goals: Successful implementation of teacher evaluation reform
examples: The UChicago Consortium surveyed all CPS teachers and principals annually across the first three years of REACH to track perceptions of fairness, usefulness, and burden.
key_sources: Sporte, S.E., & Jiang, J.Y. (2016). Teacher Evaluation in Practice: Year 3 Teacher and Administrator Perceptions of REACH. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/page/teacher-evaluation

article_title: Navigating the Shift to Intensive Principal Preparation in Illinois
citation: McIlhagga, Doug. (2016). Study Finds Successes, Challenges in Illinois Shift to Intensive Principal Preparation. Illinois Education Research Council at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. https://ierc.education
title: Balance quality and quantity when making principal preparation more selective and intensive
description: This principle, drawn from the study's lead author, holds that selective, intensive principal preparation reforms succeed only if the reduced pipeline of graduates remains sufficient to meet demand for school leaders. The study reports that preparation programs experienced substantial, but not unexpected, declines in enrollment after the shift to targeted and selective preparation, while stakeholders valued the higher quality. As Bradford R. White puts it, "Finding a balance between quality and quantity is going to be a key to the success of this policy moving forward."
requirements: Monitor whether the supply of principals prepared in more selective programs is sufficient to meet statewide demand
constraints: Enrollment declines followed the shift to selective, principal-specific preparation, per the study
target_learners: Prospective and practicing school principals in university preparation programs
target_learning_goals: School leadership capability and capacity to improve schools and raise student achievement
examples: Illinois' 2014-15 policy shift from a general administrative training model to targeted, selective principal-specific preparation across state universities
key_sources: McIlhagga, Doug. (2016). Study Finds Successes, Challenges in Illinois Shift to Intensive Principal Preparation. Illinois Education Research Council at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/navigating-shift-intensive-principal-preparation-illinois-depth-look-stakeholder

article_title: Dropout Prevention
citation: Prevention Science in School Settings chapter, edited by Kris Bosworth. (2015). Dropout Prevention: A Previously Intractable Problem Addressed Through Systems for Monitoring and Supporting Students. Springer. https://www.springer.com
title: Develop school policies and practices that prevent struggle and make supportive staff-student relationships easier to establish
description: The chapter holds that dropout prevention is not only about reacting to risk but about shaping school conditions: "Schools can develop policies and practices that make it less likely students will struggle in school, and that make it easier for school staff to establish supportive relationships with students." Prevention-oriented school design thus combines structural policy with relational support for students in the early high school years.
requirements: School staff capacity to establish supportive relationships with students
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: preventing academic struggle; graduation
examples: School-level systems in Chicago for using data to identify which students need what types of support
key_sources: Prevention Science in School Settings chapter, edited by Kris Bosworth. (2015). Dropout Prevention: A Previously Intractable Problem Addressed Through Systems for Monitoring and Supporting Students. Springer. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/dropout-prevention-previously-intractable-problem-addressed-through-systems-monitoring

article_title: Suspending Chicago's Students
citation: Sartain, L., Allensworth, E., & Porter, S. (2014). Suspending Chicago's Students: Differences in Discipline across Schools. UChicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide supportive school climates for students facing concentrated disadvantage, since suspensions cost instructional time and worsen falling behind
description: The report's authors argue that students with the most disadvantages most need a supportive school climate and too often do not get one. As co-author Elaine Allensworth states, such students are "more likely to be suspended, miss even more instructional time, and fall further behind". The principle directs schools serving high-poverty, low-achievement populations toward climate supports and alternatives to suspension, informed by the report's findings that suspensions concentrate in disadvantaged schools and associate with worse climate.
requirements: Schools must be able to implement alternative discipline approaches such as restorative justice rather than relying on suspensions
constraints: The report found policy solutions are particularly difficult to implement effectively in schools with the most disciplinary problems
target_learners: Students in high-poverty, low-achievement urban schools
African-American boys at racially diverse schools
target_learning_goals: Reducing lost instructional time
Improving school climate and peer relationships
examples: The report found almost a third of students with a history of abuse or neglect were suspended in 2013-14, and shortening suspensions was associated with improved attendance but worse climate
key_sources: Sartain, L., Allensworth, E., & Porter, S. (2014). Suspending Chicago's Students: Differences in Discipline across Schools. UChicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/suspending-chicagos-students-differences-discipline-practices-across-schools

article_title: Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools
citation: Ehrlich, S. B., Gwynne, J. A., Pareja, A. S., & Allensworth, E. M. (2014). Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools: Relationships with Learning Outcomes and Reasons for Absences. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555650
title: Schools should collect and monitor preschool attendance data at student and school levels, using monthly or biweekly watch lists to trigger outreach to families
description: The report recommends that schools systematically collect and monitor preschool attendance data as a critical first step in improving attendance. It suggests "monthly or biweekly watch lists that highlight those students who miss more than a particular number of days may prove useful, so that teachers can reach out to parents to help develop strategies for attending more regularly." Sharing attendance records with kindergarten teachers during transitions may also help maintain a consistent approach.
requirements: Attendance data must be collected and reviewed at the student and school levels on a regular basis
constraints: Schools may not be able to solve all issues that keep students from coming to school, such as poor family health or lack of access to quality medical care
target_learners: preschool students ages three and four
target_learning_goals: kindergarten readiness
regular school attendance habits
examples: The report recommends monthly or biweekly watch lists highlighting students who miss more than a particular number of days so teachers can reach out to parents, and sharing preschool attendance records with kindergarten teachers during transitions
key_sources: Ehrlich, S. B., Gwynne, J. A., Pareja, A. S., & Allensworth, E. M. (2014). Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools: Relationships with Learning Outcomes and Reasons for Absences. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555650

article_title: How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning?
citation: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr
title: Principals should make school climate the priority in school improvement efforts
description: Because the strongest mechanism linking principal leadership to schoolwide instruction and achievement is the learning climate, principals should prioritize building a safe, orderly, academically focused climate with a college-going culture. The article states that "principals need to make school climate the priority in their school improvement efforts," and that training programs preparing principals to lead urban schools must recognize this. Climate work does not require subject-specific instructional skills, making it feasible for secondary principals.
requirements: Sustained attention to safety, order, academic expectations, and a college-going culture across the whole school
constraints: Shifts toward climate must be incorporated in a way that balances principals' other roles, such as supporting quality professional development and coherent instructional programming
target_learners: high school students
students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: schoolwide instructional quality and student achievement
examples: The review recommends principals ensure the school is safe, orderly, and focused on academics, and that principals set the stage for instruction through climate, professional development opportunities, and teacher collaboration.
key_sources: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr

article_title: How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning?
citation: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr
title: Secondary principals should act as instructional leaders who organize the school for instruction, not as instructional coaches
description: The article cautions against confusing instructional leadership with instructional coaching. As instructional leaders, principals set the stage for good instruction by organizing the school to support teachers—with a safe, orderly, academically focused climate, high-quality professional development, and collaboration among teachers and with parents. Direct involvement with instruction showed "no benefits and even some detriments" for instruction quality, so the article suggests caution to leaders considering reducing organization-building time to spend more time as instructional coaches.
requirements: Principals must still support individual teacher improvement through sustained quality professional development and coherent instructional programming across departments
constraints: At the high school level, principals' direct interaction with classroom instruction may be perceived as unhelpful by teachers
target_learners: high school teachers
high school students
target_learning_goals: classroom instructional quality and student achievement
examples: The review describes principals setting the stage for instruction by ensuring an academically focused climate, professional development opportunities, and teacher and parent collaboration, rather than coaching instruction directly.
key_sources: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr

article_title: The Use of Technology in Chicago Public Schools 2011
citation: Stacy B. Ehrlich, Susan E. Sporte, and Penny Bender Sebring. (2013). The Use of Technology in Chicago Public Schools 2011: Perspectives from Students, Teachers, and Principals. UChicago CCSR Research Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/surveys/documentation
title: Increase teacher and principal technology use and expectations to raise student engagement with technology
description: The report recommends that schools seeking to increase student engagement with computers and the internet focus on the adults in the building: teacher use, teacher expectations for student use, and principal expectations and support. It states that "findings from this report suggest that increasing teacher and principal use and expectations for technology use are viable methods for increasing student engagement with computers and the internet." This rests on the observed cross-school associations between adult use, school culture, and student use.
requirements: Teachers and principals who themselves use technology regularly and set expectations for student use
constraints: The evidence is cross-sectional and associational; the report states it cannot determine the direction of the link between achievement, teacher use, and culture
target_learners: Students in grades six through 12 in large urban districts
target_learning_goals: Technological literacy
Basic technology use for school work
examples: The report highlights that students use technology more in schools where teachers also use technology more and where principals set high expectations, and flags unequal use across Chicago schools as deserving attention
key_sources: Stacy B. Ehrlich, Susan E. Sporte, and Penny Bender Sebring. (2013). The Use of Technology in Chicago Public Schools 2011: Perspectives from Students, Teachers, and Principals. UChicago CCSR Research Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/surveys/documentation

article_title: The Unintended Consequences of an Algebra-for-All Policy on High-Skill Students
citation: Algebra-for-all policy in Chicago: effects on classroom academic composition and high-skill students' math achievement. (2012). Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 34(4). https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Anticipate how schools reorganize classrooms in response to curricular mandates, because organizational responses can harm untargeted students
description: This principle holds that curricular policies such as algebra-for-all should be evaluated not only on their targeted participants but on how schools reorganize classrooms to comply. The study finds that "schools created more mixed-ability classrooms when eliminating remedial math classes," which lowered peer skill for high-skill students and, consequently, their test scores. Policy design should therefore account for composition spillovers onto students the policy does not target.
requirements: Analysis of a curricular mandate must include how schools organize classrooms to accommodate the curricular change, since little was known about this response.
constraints: Evidence comes from one district (Chicago) and one policy (1997 algebra-for-all for ninth grade), using an interrupted time-series design with within-cohort comparisons.
target_learners: Ninth-grade high school students
target_learning_goals: Algebra / mathematics achievement
examples: Chicago's 1997 policy required algebra for all ninth-graders and eliminated remedial coursework; schools responded by mixing ability levels within algebra classrooms.
key_sources: Algebra-for-all policy in Chicago: effects on classroom academic composition and high-skill students' math achievement. (2012). Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 34(4). https://journals.sagepub.com/

article_title: Want to Improve Teaching? Create Collaborative, Supportive Schools
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2012). Want to Improve Teaching? Create Collaborative, Supportive Schools. American Educator, Fall 2012. http://www.annenberginstitute.org/VUE
title: Base teacher evaluation and performance policy on school context, not individual teachers alone
description: The article argues that strategies assuming instructional quality is inherent in the teacher fail because teachers face very different working conditions; evaluation systems that "judge teachers without regard to context can further disincentivize teaching in the hardest environments." It recommends using instruction and performance data to drive conversations about practice and build professional community, and prioritizing development of collaborative relationships among teachers, leaders, and families over identifying a few effective or ineffective individuals.
requirements: Systems that support teachers around instruction, including collaboration that provides insight into better practice
constraints: Value-added and observation-based evaluation protocols commonly make no adjustments for the types of students being served; context-blind incentives risk increasing turnover in unstable schools
target_learners: Students in urban and disadvantaged schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained instructional improvement and equitable educational outcomes
examples: The article describes how data on classroom instruction and student performance can structure professional development and build a school's professional community focused on instruction and learning occurring in the building
key_sources: Elaine Allensworth. (2012). Want to Improve Teaching? Create Collaborative, Supportive Schools. American Educator, Fall 2012. http://www.annenberginstitute.org/VUE

article_title: Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago
citation: Claire Durwood, Emily Krone, and Christopher Mazzeo. (2010). Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/content/page.php?cat=3&content_id=34
title: Ability grouping can be effective when accompanied by deep supports for teachers
description: The brief argues that tracking, widely condemned for creating weak instructional environments, can benefit students when regrouping is paired with substantial instructional supports. In Chicago, "lower-skilled students benefited from more instructional time and better resources provided for their teachers," while higher-skilled students gained from more homogeneous classes. The general lesson offered is that "curriculum reforms like double-dose are more likely to succeed when they include the kinds of deep supports for teaching provided in this instance."
requirements: Extended instructional time, curricular resources, and professional development on instructional practice must accompany the regrouping
constraints: Students with the weakest skills, especially those in special education, were least well served and need differentiated support
target_learners: Ninth-grade students with below-median entering math skills
Higher-skill ninth-grade students
target_learning_goals: Algebra skills and course performance in high school mathematics
examples: Chicago schools divided freshmen by eighth-grade test scores into single-period and double-period algebra, with district professional development workshops three times a year and new curricular materials for double-dose teachers
key_sources: Claire Durwood, Emily Krone, and Christopher Mazzeo. (2010). Are Two Algebra Classes Better Than One? The Effects of Double-Dose Instruction in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/content/page.php?cat=3&content_id=34

article_title: Rethinking Teacher Evaluation
citation: Lauren Sartain, Sara Ray Stoelinga, and Emily Krone. (2010). Findings From the First Year of the Excellence in Teaching Project in Chicago Public Schools: Rethinking Teacher Evaluation. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/Joyce_TE_yr1_finaldoc.pdf
title: Provide intensive, ongoing training and support for principals when implementing observation-based evaluation systems
description: The brief's implication section argues that realizing the Danielson Framework's potential as an evaluation tool requires ongoing training and support for principals. Even with roughly 50 hours of professional development in year one, principals still struggled to rate some components consistently. The authors warn that "If scale-up to a larger number of schools does not include training and support that is intensive and ongoing, there are likely to be problematic inconsistencies in the use of the Framework by principals."
requirements: High-quality, ongoing professional development for principals, including training sessions before and during the evaluation year
constraints: Principal turnover and the difficulty of providing extensive training when an initiative expands to all schools in a large district pose legitimate challenges
target_learners: school principals serving as evaluators
target_learning_goals: accurate and consistent evaluation of instructional practice
examples: In the pilot's first year, principals received three days of summer training, four half-day professional development sessions during the year, and monthly meetings to discuss the evaluation process
key_sources: Lauren Sartain, Sara Ray Stoelinga, and Emily Krone. (2010). Findings From the First Year of the Excellence in Teaching Project in Chicago Public Schools: Rethinking Teacher Evaluation. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/Joyce_TE_yr1_finaldoc.pdf

article_title: Renaissance Schools Fund-Supported Schools
citation: Young, V. M., Humphrey, D. C., Wang, H., Bosetti, K. R., Cassidy, L., Wechsler, M. E., Rivera, E., Murray, S., & Schanzenbach, D. W. (2008). Renaissance Schools Fund-Supported Schools: Early Outcomes, Challenges, and Opportunities. SRI International. https://www.sri.com
title: Promising practices in new schools cluster in five interrelated areas: teacher capacity, data-driven decision-making, continuous instructional improvement, school culture and high expectations, and parent engagement
description: The report's case studies of RSF-supported schools organize promising practices into five areas the authors examined: "The schools’ efforts to build teacher capacity through their hiring, evaluation, and professional development practices," data use at school and classroom levels, continuous curricular and instructional improvement with remediation strategies, school culture and expectations, and parent engagement. Practices were selected for "coherence of combined practices and the depth and intensity (rather than superficiality) of those practices." The report treats these areas as interrelated rather than independent levers.
requirements: Practices were identified in schools still early in development; the report links them to future rather than current test-score gains
constraints: The report states the crucial factor is how schools use structures to strengthen instruction rather than just that the structures are in place
target_learners: K-12 students in new schools of choice in high-need urban communities
target_learning_goals: Accelerated student learning in reading and mathematics during a new school's early years
examples: Case studies across Cohort 1 schools and a subset of Cohort 2 schools over three rounds of site visits
key_sources: Young, V. M., Humphrey, D. C., Wang, H., Bosetti, K. R., Cassidy, L., Wechsler, M. E., Rivera, E., Murray, S., & Schanzenbach, D. W. (2008). Renaissance Schools Fund-Supported Schools: Early Outcomes, Challenges, and Opportunities. SRI International. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/renaissance-schools-fund-supported-schools-early-outcomes-challenges-and-opportunities

article_title: "Double-Dose" Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation
citation: Takako Nomi and Elaine M. Allensworth. (2008). “Double-dose” Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation: Effects on Students’ Academic Outcomes. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://www.informaworld.com/smpp/content~db=all?content=10.1080/19345740802676739
title: Combine regression discontinuity with interrupted time series (and instrumental variables) to estimate policy effects when the policy affects both targeted and non-targeted students
description: When a threshold-based policy changes conditions for non-targeted students too, a standard regression discontinuity cannot estimate the policy effect, only the enrollment effect. The authors show that "combining the two designs—a regression discontinuity and a time series design we address limitations that are usually inherent in each": the discontinuity provides a within-cohort check while cohort comparisons reveal effects on non-targeted students and on students far from the cutoff, with instrumental variables addressing imperfect compliance.
requirements: Pre-policy cohorts for the time-series comparison
A sharply defined eligibility cutoff as an instrument
Attention to SUTVA violations when treatment status of other students affects outcomes
constraints: Estimates are local average treatment effects among compliers and are specific to a policy year with a given level of policy compliance
target_learners: District- and system-level policy evaluators studying ninth-grade course interventions
target_learning_goals: Causal estimation of remediation-policy effects on achievement, grades, and course failure
examples: The study used the 50th-percentile cutoff as an instrument in a within-cohort IV analysis and policy year as an instrument in a cross-cohort IV analysis, estimating effects separately for each post-policy cohort
key_sources: Takako Nomi and Elaine M. Allensworth. (2008). “Double-dose” Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation: Effects on Students’ Academic Outcomes. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://www.informaworld.com/smpp/content~db=all?content=10.1080/19345740802676739

article_title: If Small Is Not Enough...?
citation: W. David Stevens. (2008). If Small Is Not Enough . . . ? The Characteristics of Successful Small High Schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Developmental practices: sustained, collective teacher work on shared instructional issues
description: Developmental practices are the report's term for improvement activities in which teachers engage in "regular group interactions focused on common instructional issues." To be coded as developmental, an activity had to be unrelated to external test preparation and meet three criteria: a focus on a specific and shared instructional issue, involvement of teachers in group work or discussion about that issue, and collaboration sustained over time through consistent meetings. Examples from the fieldwork included aligning curricula to state standards, improving student assessments, implementing differentiated instruction, and developing outcome-based learning goals.
requirements: Activities must meet the report's three criteria: shared instructional focus, group work or discussion, and sustained collaboration over time
constraints: The report distinguishes developmental practices from supportive practices, which exchange advice between pairs of teachers and address individual concerns but do not necessarily improve instruction school-wide
target_learners: high school teachers working in small schools
target_learning_goals: improving instructional quality and student course performance through collective teacher learning
examples: Paulina High's iterative development of grade-level performance expectations and Adams High's teacher-led creation of interim assessments given four times a year both met the developmental-practice criteria.
key_sources: W. David Stevens. (2008). If Small Is Not Enough . . . ? The Characteristics of Successful Small High Schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/if-small-not-enough-characteristics-successful-small-high-schools-chicago

article_title: CCSR's 2007 Survey Reports for Chicago Public Schools
citation: Luppescu, Stuart, Hart, Holly, Rosenkranz, Todd, Montgomery, Nicholas, Sporte, Susan, and Sebring, Penny Bender. (2007). Consortium on Chicago School Research 2007 Individual School Survey Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/ISR
title: Color-coded percentile-band display for comparing a school to other schools
description: The report translates each school's measure scores into a five-band color scheme so educators can see at a glance how their school compares to other CPS schools: "Red: one standard deviation or more below average (16th perc entile or lower)" through "Green: one standard deviation above average (84th percenti le or higher)". Sub-categories and the Five Fundamentals square use the same coding, and trend displays add a star position within a gray box showing the middle two-thirds of schools.
requirements: Comparison distributions from the school system and demographically similar schools, identified using test scores, enrollment, mobility, racial composition, and neighborhood characteristics
constraints: The report cautions there is unavoidable imprecision in locating the star, so small differences between a school and the system should not be over-read
target_learners: school leadership teams, teachers, and local school councils
target_learning_goals: interpreting survey-based school climate and instruction data for improvement planning
examples: Sample Elementary's Instructional Leadership is displayed as Far Above Average while Learning Climate and Instruction are Average
key_sources: Luppescu, Stuart, Hart, Holly, Rosenkranz, Todd, Montgomery, Nicholas, Sporte, Susan, and Sebring, Penny Bender. (2007). Consortium on Chicago School Research 2007 Individual School Survey Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/ISR

article_title: Educating for Democracy
citation: Susan E. Sporte and Joseph E. Kahne. (2007). Educating for Democracy: Lessons from Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research Research Brief. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Embed civic best practices across the curriculum rather than relying on required civics courses
description: The article concludes that requiring courses in American Government may help but will not guarantee the learning opportunities found most important. Instead, "policymakers and educators need to look for ways to embed 'best practices' into classrooms by highlighting the importance of these practices and related civic outcomes, as well as through curriculum and professional development opportunities." These practices—service learning, open discussion of controversial issues, and community problem solving—can take place in any class, including art, English, or science.
requirements: Classroom practices must actually occur in classrooms; merely offering a civics or government course is not enough, since prior studies assessing only course offering found no relationship.
constraints: The authors note more than one-third of Chicago students reported not discussing issues they care about in any class over the year, showing these practices are not yet widespread.
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: commitment to civic participation
community problem solving
examples: An art teacher at Excel Academy had students investigate and reflect on school violence and create a poster campaign promoting peace; an English teacher at Lakeview High School held open discussions in which students questioned him, each other, and sources; an environmental science class at the School of Social Justice studied electrical power generation and local environmental justice issues.
key_sources: Susan E. Sporte and Joseph E. Kahne. (2007). Educating for Democracy: Lessons from Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research Research Brief. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educating-democracy-lessons-chicago

article_title: Keeping New Teachers
citation: Lura Forcum and William Harms. (2005). New report shows that high-quality induction can help keep teachers on the job. University of Chicago press release announcing Keeping New Teachers: A First Look at the Influence of Induction in the Chicago Public Schools. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide high-quality induction combining mentoring, observation with feedback, guidance on rules and procedures, and classroom management support to keep new teachers
description: The article's central design recommendation is that new teachers receive high-quality induction rather than mere program participation. High-quality induction includes "mentoring activities such as observation of and feedback on their teaching; guidance with regard to CPS rules, policies, and procedures; and classroom management strategies." Novices receiving such induction are more likely to intend to continue teaching and report a good experience, and combined intensive mentoring and support shows the largest retention-plan differences.
requirements: Induction must include mentoring with observation of and feedback on teaching, guidance on district rules, policies, and procedures, and classroom management strategies.
Supports such as scheduled collaboration, teacher networks, release time to observe, and principal encouragement should accompany mentoring.
constraints: Participation in an induction program alone does not improve the chances teachers will remain; quality, not mere participation, is what matters.
The high school mentoring relationship was similar but not statistically significant.
target_learners: novice elementary and high school teachers in Chicago Public Schools, including career changers
target_learning_goals: teacher retention in the profession
a good early teaching experience
plans to remain in the same school
examples: The report compared novice teachers who received strong versus weak levels of mentoring and other supports on three outcomes: reporting a good experience, intending to continue teaching, and planning to remain in the same school.

University of Chicago press release announcing Keeping New Teachers: A First Look at the Influence of Induction in the Chicago Public Schools. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: The Essential Supports for School Improvement
citation: Sebring, P. B., Allensworth, E., Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., & Luppescu, S. (2006). The Essential Supports for School Improvement. Research Report, Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Pursue school improvement holistically across all essential supports rather than through narrow interventions
description: Because strength in multiple essential supports is what produces improvement, the report argues that narrow, single-focus interventions will have limited success. It states that "narrow interventions will have limited success in improving student learning," giving the example that technology investments will have little effect if students do not feel safe and classrooms are frequently disrupted. The framework therefore embraces a holistic, coherent view of school development in which all five supports are strengthened together and focused on ambitious instruction.
requirements: Attention to all five essential supports, since a weakness in any organizational element can undermine strengths in other areas
constraints: Derived from Chicago elementary school evidence, 1990-1996; the report notes schools with high concentrations of students with extraordinary needs had few resources remaining to sustain improvement efforts
target_learners: Elementary school students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: Raising student academic achievement through coordinated school development
examples: The report cites investments in integrating technology into the curriculum as having little effect when students do not feel safe and classrooms face frequent disruptions
key_sources: Sebring, P. B., Allensworth, E., Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., & Luppescu, S. (2006). The Essential Supports for School Improvement. Research Report, Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/essential-supports-school-improvement

article_title: Teaching Adolescents to Become Learners
citation: Farrington, C.A., Roderick, M., Allensworth, E., Nagaoka, J., Keyes, T.S., Johnson, D.W., & Beechum, N.O. (2012). Teaching adolescents to become learners. The role of noncognitive factors in shaping school performance: A critical literature review. Chicago: University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Evaluate noncognitive-factor evidence for actionability: malleability, classroom context, and teacher strategies
description: The review argues identification alone is insufficient for practice: "Validating the claim that schools would get high payoffs from working on noncognitive factors requires an evaluation of whether the supporting evidence is 'actionable' for practitioners." Evidence is actionable only when the factor is shown to be malleable, shown to be affected by classroom context, and accompanied by research-based strategies teachers can use within regular instruction. Practitioners would ideally also track change in the targeted factor.
requirements: Randomized experimental designs that show interventions change both the factor and grades, plus clarity about mechanisms rather than leaving a black box
constraints: Much existing research is correlational, and mechanisms of change in experiments often cannot be observed
target_learners: Adolescent students in middle grades, high school, and transition to college
target_learning_goals: Course grades and development of noncognitive factors
examples: For each of the five categories the review asks how the factor relates to grades, whether it is malleable, what role classroom context plays, whether actionable strategies exist, and whether changing it would narrow gender or race/ethnicity gaps
key_sources: Farrington, C.A., Roderick, M., Allensworth, E., Nagaoka, J., Keyes, T.S., Johnson, D.W., & Beechum, N.O. (2012). Teaching adolescents to become learners. The role of noncognitive factors in shaping school performance: A critical literature review. article_title: Professional Communities and Instructional Improvement Practices
citation: Stevens, W. D., with Kahne, J. (2006). Professional Communities and Instructional Improvement Practices: A study of small high schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Support teacher professional communities by making instructional discussion a regular, formally led part of meetings
description: The report recommends that schools create common meeting time and then go beyond it: "teacher teams need to make instructional discussions a regular and formal part of their meetings," with routines and processes ensuring sustained and systematic attention to instructional practices. Meeting time alone is described as necessary but insufficient, since daily pressures can easily distract teachers from instructional improvement issues. The report also calls for identifying administrative and teacher leaders responsible for directing attention to systematic improvement of core instructional practices.
requirements: Common meeting time must be paired with formalized instructional discussion routines and identified leadership, since regular meeting times alone do not eliminate the pressures that distract teachers
constraints: Creating common meeting time is a necessary, but insufficient, step toward helping teachers work together on instruction
target_learners: High school teachers in small schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained collective improvement of core instructional practices
examples: In school C, the principal and lead teacher initiated recurring professional development workshops around developing a standards-based curriculum, which prompted sustained collective discussions about instruction

Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/professional-communities-and-instructional-improvement-practices-study-small-high

article_title: Still Crazy after All These Years
citation: Payne, Charles. (2005). Still Crazy after All These Years: Race in the Chicago School System. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Illinois at Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: External partners and reform programs should respect and draw on local educators' knowledge rather than imposing models
description: Payne argues school reform programs fail when developers treat local professionals as mere implementers. Quoting superintendent James Lytle's interview, "Nearly all of them are disdainful in their attitudes toward local educators," and Lytle's "McDonald's approach" analogy, Payne likens reformers to colonists who explain all failures in terms of local limitations. He further argues, citing Delpit, that universalist models devalue knowledge nonwhite professionals hold from culture and locality.
requirements: Reform designs must leave room for local professionals to contribute "over and above the model design."
constraints: Payne notes teachers of color can also exaggerate how much relevant knowledge they have; claims of special insight must be examined for self-service.
target_learners: urban school staff and educators in demoralized, high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: building school capacity for improvement through respectful external partnership
examples: Payne's account of elite-educated interns who had to unlearn institutional arrogance and signify "I just work there" to work effectively in black institutions in Chicago.
key_sources: Payne, Charles. (2005). Still Crazy after All These Years: Race in the Chicago School System. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Illinois at Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/still-crazy-after-all-these-years-race-chicago-school-system

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Improving Chicago's Schools: Sample High School Summary 2005. (2005). UChicago Consortium on School Data Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use school-specific survey reports to help a school assess its progress and plan for the future
description: The article presents the school-specific survey reports as a tool for school self-assessment and improvement planning. The reports describe a school's learning climate, instructional program, student-teacher relationships, leadership, professional environment, and community relationships. The article states that "this information about where a school is and how it is developing can help the school assess its progress and plan for the future."
requirements: Schools must meet the participation thresholds (at least 42 percent of teachers or 50 percent of students) to receive reports
target_learners: K-12 school communities in Chicago public schools
target_learning_goals: school improvement planning
school climate assessment
examples: Summary reports show responses on survey measures over several years; details reports show answers to specific survey questions compared across schools

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Quartile-benchmarked category reporting format compares a school's responses to bottom- and top-quartile schools with defined category descriptions
description: Each measure is reported as a horizontal bar figure showing the percentage of respondents endorsing each survey item, with a diamond marking the systemwide average, followed by a frequency distribution placing the school's responses among four defined categories alongside bottom-quartile and top-quartile schools. Schools are divided 'into four equally sized categories (quartiles) based on their responses to each set of questions,' and each category (e.g., minimal, limited, moderate, extensive) is defined in detail in an accompanying table. Bars exceeding 65 percent extend to the top of the axis without a value label.
requirements: A sufficient response rate for the school and item-level response counts to compute percentages
constraints: The schools in each quartile varied for every set of questions, so a school can be top quartile on one measure and bottom quartile on another; bars above 65 percent are not given value labels
target_learners: school principals, teachers, and Local School Councils conducting self-assessment
target_learning_goals: interpreting school climate and instructional program measures
examples: For Teacher Influence, the report explains that 23 percent of teachers in bottom-quartile schools considered their influence minimal, compared with 4 percent in top-quartile schools and 9 percent in the sample school
key_sources: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-sample-high-school-details-2005

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: School survey profiles comparing a school to demographically similar schools and system trends over time
description: The report's display format charts a school's score on each measure across five survey years alongside two reference trends. It "compares your school both to other schools that are demographically similar to yours, and to the Chicago public school system as a whole," with a gray box marking the middle two-thirds of schools and a star locating the school's standing. Time-trend data show whether reform efforts are improving, and trend bands distinguish somewhat from substantially above- or below-average reports.
requirements: Multiple years of survey participation to display trends; at least seven respondents per measure for a valid school reading
constraints: Star placement carries unavoidable imprecision, so small differences between the school and reference lines should not be over-read; a school's own data may be missing for some years
target_learners: school leadership teams, principals, teachers, and Local School Councils
target_learning_goals: school self-assessment and improvement planning
examples: The illustrative Program Coherence display charts 1994-2003 trends with the school's line, a schools-like-yours dashed line, and the systemwide solid line

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use multi-measure school survey reports to support self-assessment and improvement planning
description: The report is designed to supplement test-score data in school improvement planning: it is "intended to supplement your assessments of test-score data and other performance indicators on the School Improvement Plan for Advancing Academic Achievement." By identifying areas that are strong, weak, strengthening, or weakening over time, the profiles can stimulate discussion among the principal, teachers, and Local School Council about priorities, partnerships, community resources, and student safety.

constraints: Measure definitions indicate whether items are positive or negative measures; on Incidence of Disciplinary Action, low scores are desirable

target_learning_goals: setting improvement priorities and planning school development
examples: The report provides guiding questions under each profile, such as whether school improvement efforts over the last two years reflect a coordinated plan

article_title: Educational Technology
citation: Holly M. Hart, Elaine Allensworth, Douglas L. Lauen, Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Educational Technology: Availability and Use in Chicago's Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Provide adequate resources and develop teachers' capacity to integrate technology as the two most important supports
description: The article recommends that creating technology-rich learning environments requires securing adequate computing hardware and human resource support, and building teachers' individual capacity through time for training, principal leadership, and a professional community. It states "The two most important are adequate resources and the development of teachers' capacity to integrate technology well." Teachers value professional development that produces classroom-ready lessons and models techniques collaboratively.
requirements: Time to participate in training and to evaluate new ideas
Principal leadership to provide goals and secure resources
A professional community where teachers can collaborate and learn together
constraints: The typical CPS school had yet to secure adequate computing hardware and human resource support
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public school districts
target_learning_goals: Regular, meaningful instructional use of computers and the Internet
examples: The brief describes an on-site technical coordinator who ensures reliable access to working hardware and software, identifies professional development, and advises teachers before, during, and after implementation

Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educational-technology-its-availability-and-use-chicagos-public-schools

article_title: Educational Technology
citation: Holly M. Hart, Elaine Allensworth, Douglas L. Lauen, Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Educational Technology: Availability and Use in Chicago's Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Transparent technology use embedded in authentic project tasks
description: The article presents a lesson-level pattern in which technology serves an instructional goal naturally rather than as an add-on: in a collaborative recycling project, student groups use digital cameras for peer interviews, produce educational videos, survey classrooms and analyze data into graphs and charts, and design a web page. The authors call this "transparent technology use" that services the instruction goal "in a way that is natural and endemic rather than being an awkward addition to an old task."
requirements: Sufficient access to the needed devices and software for multiple concurrent student groups
target_learners: Elementary and secondary students in project-based classrooms
target_learning_goals: Data collection and analysis, communication of findings, and collaborative inquiry
examples: Two teachers collaborated on a recycling project in which four student groups used cameras, video production, survey data analysis, and web page design

article_title: Research and Evaluation in the Chicago Public Schools
citation: Laurence Stanton and John Q. Easton. (2002). Research and Evaluation in the Chicago Public Schools: A Plan for the Future. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/research-and-evaluation-chicago-public-schools-plan-future
title: Locate the research and evaluation department so it reports directly to the chief executive to support independence and honest information
description: The report recommends that DRE "maintain its relative independence within the CPS by reporting directly to the CEO." Interviewees and committee members agreed that direct reporting "increases the likelihood that information and knowledge will inform district pol- icy" and that separating DRE from the departments operating the programs it evaluates "supports DRE's inde- pendence and its ability to be honest."
requirements: Department leadership with standing to deliver unwelcome news; separation from the operating departments it evaluates
constraints: The report notes the inherent difficulty of providing the system's leadership with news that it does not want to hear
target_learners: District and school leaders who use research to inform policy
target_learning_goals: Accurate information about program strengths and weaknesses to support mid-course adjustments
examples: Since October 2001, DRE reported directly to CEO Duncan rather than to the Accountability Office to which it previously reported
